paper.title: Brothers increase women’s gender conformity
paper.code_data_availability: Data availability: ‘The data that I use in this paper are based on several Danish administrative registers. …

registers.name_in_paper: Danish administrative data for the total population (unnamed registers held at Statistics Denmark)
registers.role: sample frame, treatment (sibling sex), family linkage, controls and most outcomes
variables_mentioned: parents’ length, type and field of education
parents’ labor market attachment and occupation
family structure observed on January 1 each year

registers.name_in_paper: DISCO, the Danish version of the International Standard Classification of Occupations
registers.role: outcomes: four-digit occupation codes used to build the male share in the woman’s own occupation, the STEM-occupation indicator and the female share in the partner’s occupation
outcomes and subgroup definition: hours-based labor supply, used to measure cumulated lifetime work experience and parents’ division of labor during childhood
variables_mentioned: employer contributions based on the number of hours worked

registers.role: outcomes and controls: labor earnings (percentile by age and cohort, levels and logs) and dummies for the number of years observed in the income registry from ages 31 to 40
outcomes and controls: highest completed education, STEM enrollment and completion, and age at last observation in the education registry

registers.name_in_paper: Grade 9 written exam grades (externally graded, in Danish and Math)
registers.role: outcomes: own and next-generation school performance, standardized by exam year for the entire student population

registers.name_in_paper: the Danish Longitudinal Survey of Children (DALSC), linked to administrative data
registers.role: outcomes: parental quality-time investment at child ages 7 and 11 and the quality of child-parent and child-sibling relations
variables_mentioned: how often each parent plays with the child

linkages: all children linked to their parents, siblings, (cohabiting and marital) partners, and own children, so that parents’ complete fertility history and thereby the sibling sex composition are correctly measured
the partner defined as the mode person with whom the woman cohabits or is married between the ages of 31 and 41
the school performance of the grandchildren observed through the women’s own first-born children
the DALSC survey linked to the administrative data

sample.universe: the total Danish population observed in administrative data from 1980 to 2016
sample.unit_of_observation: first-born woman (one observation per woman); woman-by-event-year for the event studies of the response to motherhood and of ages 18–40; first-born child of the woman for the next-generation analysis
selection_rules: only first-born women, who are the first child to both the mother and father
immigrants excluded (first-generation immigrants lack complete sibling or parental information; second-generation immigrants, about 1% of the sample, excluded for homogeneity)
only individuals who have at least one full sibling (same mother and father) born less than 4 years apart and who survived the first year of life (72% of those fulfilling all other requirements)
families in which either the first or second child is a twin excluded
women who died before the age of 40 or did not live in Denmark at any time between the ages of 31 and 40 excluded
for the event studies of labor market outcomes: women living outside Denmark for at most 3 years of the analysis period

DALSC analyses: first-born girls born September–October 1995 to a mother with Danish citizenship with a second-born sibling born within 5 years (spacing allowed within 5 rather than 4 years to increase power)
next-generation analyses: first-born children of the main sample born 1987–2000 with an observed Grade 9 written exam grade
own Grade 9 analyses: girls born 1986–1999 with the same selection criteria as the main sample
sample.n_observations: 103,771 first-born women in the main sample (50,757 with a second-born sister and 53,014 with a second-born brother); 95,058 with an identified partner; 611/586 maternal and 444/434 paternal reports at child ages 7/11 in the DALSC sample
sample.n_individuals: 103,771 first-born women in the main sample

construction_notes: all binary variables (variables measuring shares) are multiplied by 100 to express percent (percentage points); in the regression tables the stated estimates are multiplied by 100 to express effects in log/percentage points or percent of a standard deviation
the male share in the woman’s own occupation and the female share in the partner’s occupation are used in logarithms because these measures best approximate a normal distribution

occupational outcomes of the first-born women are measured as a mean from ages 31 to 40; the partner’s occupational outcome is measured mainly at the partner’s ages 31–45 for the partner with whom the woman lived for most years from ages 31 to 41
DISCO occupation codes are observed from 1991 to 2013, so occupation is only observed through age 38 (39) for the 1975 (1974) cohort
work experience is cumulated lifetime full-time equivalent experience in months at the end of each calendar year; un- and non-employment do not count while maternity and parental leave spells do
earnings are measured as the earnings percentile by age and cohort, constructed on the total population; log earnings are the natural logarithm of labor earnings in 1000 DKK 2015-prices
GPA measures are standardized by (track and) year of graduation for the total population with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1

parental quality-time investment is a principal-component index of five weekly activities (playing, homework, out-of-school activities, reading/singing, excursions), standardized to mean 0 and SD 1; each individual component is also standardized to mean 0 and SD 1
child-parent and child-sibling relationship indexes are first principal components standardized so that a higher value reflects a better relationship (mean 0, SD 1)

‘parents working equally’ (non-traditional family) is the tertile of families in which the parents’ division of labor until the child turns 19 years is most equal; fathers in this group work at most 62% of the total parental labor supply, measured through the ATP pension scheme
family structure is observed on January 1 each year, using the observation for the year when the person turns 18 or the last year in which the child lived with at least one biological parent
if a parent does not have a field-specific education, their field of occupation is used for the parental level-by-field of education fixed effects

the relative earnings difference in the couple is the difference between the partner’s and the woman’s labor earnings as a share of the couple’s total earnings during the first five years the couple lives together when the woman is 31–40 years; age to partner is set to 0 if the woman is older than the partner

links.pointer_quote: Specifically, women with a brother work in more female-dominated occupations during their thirties and choose more traditional partners.

claims.statement: Having a second-born brother rather than a sister reduces the male share in the occupation first-born women work in during their thirties.

definition.value: Indicator equal to one if the woman’s second-born biological sibling (same mother and father), born less than 4 years after her, is male rather than female; the omitted category is a second-born sister

timing.value: Realised at the birth of the second-born sibling, on average 2.5 years (29.9–30.0 months) after the woman’s own birth

register_source.value: DISCO, the Danish version of the International Standard Classification of Occupations, observed from 1991 to 2013 (four-digit occupation codes); no DST register code is given

definition.value: The natural logarithm of the average male share in the woman’s four-digit occupation codes observed between the ages of 31 and 40; estimates are multiplied by 100 to express effects in log/percentage points

timing.value: mean over ages 31–40

units.value: log points (the estimate is multiplied by 100 to express log points)

magnitude.interpretation: The paper describes the corresponding raw difference (column (1)) as women with a brother working ‘in occupations with 1.2% fewer men’ than women with a sister

estimand.target_population: First-born women born 1962–1975 with a second-born biological sibling born within 4 years (the main sample)
estimand.time_horizon: occupational outcome measured as a mean from ages 31 to 40
estimand.formal_query: E[Y|do(SecondBornBrother=1)] − E[Y|do(SecondBornBrother=0)] for first-born women with a second-born sibling born within 4 years

population.description: Main sample: first-born women born in Denmark 1962–1975 who are the first child to both mother and father, with at least one full sibling (same mother and father) born less than 4 years apart who survived the first year of life; immigrants, families in which the first or second child is a twin, and women who died before age 40 or did not live in Denmark at any time between ages 31 and 40 are excluded
population.ages: outcomes measured in their thirties (ages 31–40) and through age 41
subgroups_defined: parental division of labor during childhood (parents working (almost) equally — the most equal tertile, fathers working at most 62% of total parental labor supply — vs. unequal)
parental field of academic education (mother in care or administration; father in STEM)
parental years of education (mother and/or father ≥ 12 years)
spacing to the second-born sibling (<2, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6–8 years)
population.selection: Conditioned on the parents having a second child within 4 years, on the first child being a daughter, on survival to age 40 and on living in Denmark at some time between ages 31 and 40; the paper states that sibling sex composition does not affect attrition due to these restrictions

identification.source_of_variation: Random assignment of the sex of the second-born child in families whose first-born child is a daughter, conditional on the parents having a second child: parents do not know the sex of an unborn child when they decide to have another child

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the first child being a daughter and on the parents having a second child, the sex of the second child is random, i.e. unrelated to predetermined family characteristics and to potential outcomes
key_assumptions.supported_by: t-tests of predetermined family background characteristics by sibling sex and a joint F-test that the control variables in Xi cannot predict having a second-born brother (Table 1, joint F-statistic 0.92, Prob > F 0.92)

heterogeneity.dimension: parental division of labor during childhood (parents working (almost) equally vs. unequally), Table 4 panel A
heterogeneity.finding: the effect of having a brother on occupational choice disappears for women coming from more gender-equal families: the interaction SBB × Equal is 1.72 (SE 1.01) for log(male share in own occupation), −0.03 (SE 0.25) for the share of years in STEM occupation and −0.03 (SE 1.42) for log(female share in partner's occupation)

heterogeneity.dimension: parental field of academic education, Table 4 panel B
heterogeneity.finding: the effect of having a brother is strongest for those women with more traditional parents in terms of their educational field; the effects seem to be largest in magnitude for those with a mother who has an academic education within care or administration (SBB × Mother Care/Adm = −1.01, SE 0.35, for the STEM-occupation outcome) and for those with a father who has an academic education within STEM (SBB × Father STEM = −3.79, SE 2.04, for log(male share in own occupation))

heterogeneity.dimension: parental years of education, Table 4 panel C
heterogeneity.finding: the effect of having a brother is largest for those with at least one highly educated parent (≥12 years of education) for occupational choice; women whose parents both have less education do not experience an effect of sibling sex

heterogeneity.dimension: spacing to the second-born sibling, Appendix Fig. 3
heterogeneity.finding: sibling sex does not have an impact for those with long spacing between them and their sibling; however, the estimated effects by spacing are not statistically significantly different from each other
